content.text: Technical Review Stage | Lead Forward Deployed Engineer | 2:30pm Today

"I'm a hands-on engineer who builds production AI systems end-to-end, from RAG pipelines to cloud deployments. I don't start with technology; I understand the business problem, validate quickly with prototypes, make pragmatic trade-offs, communicate clearly to stakeholders, and own the outcome through to production."

Built a polyglot RAG chat app with Next.js 16 frontend, Python FastAPI backend, Convex real-time database, and multi-provider LLM orchestration via LangChain, deployed to GCP Cloud Run with Terraform IaC.

Implemented full RAG pipeline: 500-char recursive chunking, MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings with multi-provider fallback, Convex vector search, and context injection with source citation and 0.6 similarity threshold.

Chose polyglot (TypeScript + Python) because LangChain's Python libraries have richer AI orchestration, while Next.js excels at UI/auth; Convex gives real-time sync and built-in vector search in one database.

Trade-off: 500-char chunks hit the sweet spot (smaller lost context, larger diluted retrieval accuracy); challenge was embedding provider credits depleting, solved with FallbackEmbedder that auto-switches between HuggingFace, OpenAI, and Google.

Using multiple programming languages in one system, each chosen for what it does best; in my project, TypeScript handles the UI/auth (Next.js excels here) and Python handles AI orchestration (LangChain's ecosystem is richer in Python).

Retrieval-Augmented Generation: instead of relying solely on the LLM's training data, we retrieve relevant documents first, then augment the prompt with that context before the model generates a response.

body: R - Retrieval
Query knowledge base to find relevant chunks
Vector similarity search in Convex with 0.6 threshold
A - Augmentation
Inject retrieved context into the LLM prompt
Context block with source names and relevance scores
G - Generation
LLM generates response grounded in that context
LangChain chain with streaming + source citation prompt

content.text: "RAG lets the AI answer questions using your company's documents, not just what it learned during training."
A reactive real-time database with built-in vector search; data syncs instantly to all connected clients without polling or WebSockets boilerplate.
Convex is a managed serverless platform that auto-scales; I don't provision servers, it handles concurrency, and vector indexes are built-in so no separate Pinecone/Weaviate to manage.
Both a React Native app and Next.js web app can subscribe to the same Convex queries; when a message is saved, both apps see it instantly without me writing sync logic.

Convex has native vector search (384-dim index built-in) and TypeScript-first schema; Supabase would need pgvector extension, Firebase has no vector support, both require more glue code for real-time.
Server Components reduce client bundle size, App Router gives clean file-based routing, and it's the React meta-framework with the best Vercel/edge deployment story.

Next.js has the largest ecosystem (shadcn/ui, Clerk auth, Convex SDK all have first-class Next support); Remix is great but smaller community, Nuxt is Vue (I'm faster in React), SvelteKit is emerging but fewer production case studies.
LangChain's Python library has deeper integrations (LangSmith tracing, more provider SDKs, agentic patterns) and the ML/AI ecosystem (PyTorch, HuggingFace Transformers) is Python-native.

body: LangChain Python has LangGraph, eval harnesses, callbacks
LangChain.js is lighter, fewer features
HuggingFace Transformers runs natively
Node needs ONNX or API calls
FastAPI matches NestJS DX with less boilerplate
NestJS is great but AI libs are weaker
Data scientists speak Python
Hiring AI talent is easier with Python

content.text: "I could have built this in Node, but I'd have spent more time fighting the ecosystem; Python let me focus on the product, not the plumbing."
I use Factory Droid daily as a pair programmer: AI suggests code, I review every line, understand the "why," test thoroughly, and make final architecture decisions myself.
I never commit without understanding the code; I run type checks (tsc --noEmit), verify edge cases, and ask the AI to explain unfamiliar patterns before accepting them.
At Grapple Law, AI suggested an n8n workflow that would have created duplicate Stripe webhooks; I caught it during review and refactored to idempotent handlers, preventing double-billing.

At BBC News, the stated request was "rewrite articles with AI," but the actual problem was journalists couldn't trust AI output; I built a diff-comparison UI so they could review and selectively accept changes.
Before designing, I always ask: Who are the users? What does success look like? What are the accuracy, latency, and cost constraints? What happens when the AI gets it wrong?
Translating technical decisions into business impact:

I explain RAG chunking to execs as: "We're teaching the AI to find needles in haystacks by cutting documents into small, searchable pieces, which means faster, more accurate answers from your knowledge base."

At Grapple Law, the founder wanted to ship AI features before testing; I presented data showing 15% hallucination rate in legal advice, proposed a one-week eval sprint, and we shipped with confidence scoring that saved client trust.
Explaining a complex technical issue simply:
I describe vector embeddings as: "We turn words into coordinates on a map, so similar meanings are close together, and the AI can find related documents by measuring distance."
At UK DCMS, the PM wanted to migrate everything at once; I proposed incremental migration with feature flags, showed the rollback risk of big-bang deploys, and we shipped safely over 3 sprints.

Embedding API credits kept depleting mid-conversation; I built a FallbackEmbedder factory that automatically tries OpenAI, then HuggingFace, then Google, so RAG never breaks even when one provider is down.
A project that went wrong and how you recovered:
At Grapple Law, a Docker build took 12+ minutes and caused CI timeouts; I identified the bottleneck (no layer caching), introduced blacksmith.sh caching, and cut builds to under 3 minutes.
In the RAG project, I noticed no input validation; I added 4000-char limits and prompt injection detection before launch, preventing potential abuse.
A mistake/failure and what you learned:
Early in my RAG work, I used 1000-char chunks and retrieval accuracy was poor; I learned that smaller chunks (500) with overlap maintain semantic boundaries and improve precision.
At Goat Interactive, I prototyped 3 Next.js apps in 2 weeks, then productionised with Terraform, Kubernetes, and ArgoCD; shipped to 28 countries with proper CI/CD, observability, and scaling.

At Grapple Law, I co-led a 24/7 AI legal service; when press coverage spiked traffic 10x, I scaled DigitalOcean droplets within hours and communicated status updates directly to the founder every 30 minutes.

For my take-home, the brief was "build something with RAG"; I framed it as a knowledge base chat, defined success metrics (retrieval accuracy, response grounding), and delivered a production-ready system with LangSmith observability.
Who are the users? What problem are we solving? What data is available? What are the privacy/security requirements? What accuracy is acceptable? How will we measure success?
I'd propose a working prototype in one week to validate value (e.g., basic RAG with off-the-shelf embeddings), then iterate based on user feedback before productionising.

body: What's polyglot?
Multiple languages in one system, each doing what it's best at
What's RAG?
Retrieve docs → Augment prompt → Generate grounded response
Why Convex?
Real-time sync + built-in vector search, no separate DB to manage
Why Next.js?
Best React ecosystem, Server Components, clean App Router
Why Python?
LangChain is richer, AI/ML ecosystem is Python-native
